label: relief-cuts-rev/sand-steps/stairs-h1-w2

surfaces.part: stair cut / cliff face below lip

answer.evidence: Rows 0-15 form a flat sand terrace band, width 32 across all rows. It ends in a bright 1-row lip line at row 16 (#fff9b4 in all three scanned columns). Below it, rows 17-30 form a lighter, separate recessed face. It has stepped tone changes at rows 17-21 and a shadow line at rows 26 and 30, so it reads as the cut face or stair run descending from the lip. The terrace band is 16 rows, far more than a rim, and the face below is 14 rows. No isometric side face is drawn. The tile is somewhat ambiguous because the stairs are meant to be seen from above, but the structure matches a top surface with an edge line above a front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate reads as a sand block cut into horizontal bands. Each stair step has a light top edge, a mid-sand face and a darker brown lip, which gives about 4 lightness steps against roughly 6 on the references. Outlines and step edges lean brown, so they are dark material tone, which matches the 0% near-neutral edge fact. The measured 6 visible tones per tile is close to the paving reference (7) and above the grass (3), so the numbers alone do not fail it. By eye, though, the step faces are broad runs of one sand colour with only a few sparse speckle dots. The 16% near-flat coverage confirms this against 0% on both references. There is no per-grain sand texture, no stippling or pebbles, and no per-step shading variation like the stone-by-stone shading and tuft clusters in the references. It also has only 7 raw colours, versus 26 per tile on the grass. It looks flatter and simpler than the references, and with the stairs reading only weakly, a careful artist would not accept it next to them.

surfaces.part: upper step riser / cliff face (darker sand)

answer.evidence: The tile is 32 rows tall and fully opaque, drawn as two stacked bands. Rows 3-15 are a darker, uniform sand face of about 13 rows, which I read as the vertical riser or cliff face. It is bounded above by the highlight lip at rows 0-2 and below by a bright edge line at row 16. Rows 17-29 are a lighter, speckled sand band of 13 rows, which I read as the horizontal tread. It ends in a darker edge line at row 30 and a highlight at row 31. The 13-row tread is a real horizontal surface and the 13-row riser is a vertical face, so the tile reads as a stepped three-quarter form, not a single flat slab. Confidence is moderate, because the texture is flat and the edge lines sit at the top of each band rather than the bottom.
